executive_summary: CAD/CHF closed at 0.58158 on 2026-10-02. The pair is quoted as Swiss francs per Canadian dollar, so a rising pair means a stronger Canadian dollar. Over the last month the pair is down 0.68%. It is up 2.15% over three months, 1.65% over six months and 2.52% over a year, and it sits at the 68th percentile of its 52-week closing range of 0.56308-0.59041. The cross pits two currencies that are each scored Bearish in their own dossiers. CAD's main support is a 225bp policy-rate lead, which pays 268.6bp a year on a rolled futures position. Against that, Canada is the weaker leg on almost everything else: Q2 growth was 0.82% q/q against Switzerland's 1.885%, Canada's current-account surplus is 8.17pp of GDP smaller, and Canada is absorbing US import bans that took effect on 2026-09-29. The front-end asymmetry also runs against CAD: the Canadian two-year carries about 112bp of priced rate hikes above its policy rate, against about 31bp in Switzerland, and the Bank of Canada must publish an oil assumption on 2026-10-28 while the SNB says nothing until 2026-12-10. The settled verdict is Tactical Neutral (score +0.0706, conviction 2) and Strategic Bearish (score -0.1350, conviction 2). The chart broke down just as the verdict was struck: the pair fell about 120 pips over 2026-10-01 and 2026-10-02, closed below its 50-day average at 0.58331, broke the sequence of higher lows that ran from July to September, and is now inside a thin two-touch band (0.57811-0.58232). Below that, the 200-day average sits inside a three-touch support zone at 0.5717-0.5762. We disagree with the tactical Neutral in one respect. It was scored on a calm risk backdrop, and since then the OAT-Bund spread reached around 140.6bp after Reuters recorded 132.86bp on October 1, already its widest since the 2012 eurozone debt crisis, and Swiss September CPI rose 1.0% year-on-year. We therefore see near-term risk tilted to the downside. That view shows up in a slightly negative scenario expected value, not in the score. For the strategic view, the caveat is the cost of carry: a spot short pays about 78 pips of roll over six months, which leaves the expected value close to zero if entered at spot. We prefer selling rallies into 0.5865-0.5875, or expressing the view through the legs.

market_context.valuation_assessment: Both dossiers build a REER-relative proxy from the BIS broad real effective exchange rates for 2026-08: CAD at 96.29 (down 1.67 points year on year) and CHF at 99.87 (down 2.83% year on year). The REERs are monthly and have not been updated for the move since, so measured against today's 0.58158 the gap is about 4.8%. This is a base-period deviation, not true purchasing-power parity, and it does not trigger mean reversion at either horizon. The more telling structural fact is the 200-week average at 0.62302. Spot has not closed above it for 204 weeks, and it is declining by 7.55 pips a week. The pair has been in a multi-year downtrend driven by CAD weakness against CHF since late 2022. The current level is a rebound inside that downtrend, not a break of it. The market is pricing a persistent discount on Canadian trade and growth and no premium for Switzerland's 9.198%-of-GDP surplus. Neither currency's external position is being capitalised.

market_context.recent_regime: Until 2026-09-30 the cross was a textbook carry grind. The franc was the funding leg: OCBC argued the SNB is unlikely to validate the market's relatively hawkish pricing, expecting rates unchanged well into 2027 while OIS prices a meaningful December hike probability. The pair rose from the 0.565 area in early July to 0.5915 on 2026-09-17. That regime broke over two sessions when three franc-positive shocks coincided: France unveiled a EUR 43 billion austerity package on October 1 and the spread blew out; Swiss core CPI rose to 0.5% YoY in September from 0.4%; and weak US payrolls reportedly cut implied odds of an October Fed move from 70% to below 20%, which took away the dollar-side support for franc weakness. On the Canadian side, the US ban on various Canadian goods imports also took effect. The dominant narrative is therefore moving from 'franc as funding currency' to 'franc as eurozone refuge'. That is exactly the tail that pass 1's Factor 3 strategic Neutral was built to accommodate.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The Bank of Canada's Overnight Rate Target of 2.25% sits 225bp above the SNB Policy Rate of 0.00%, which is CAD's largest carry advantage anywhere in its G10 set and, from the franc side, one of the least punitive short-franc legs available. The gated payload puts the ten-year differential at +320.5bp in CAD's favour, though both legs are monthly observations as of 2026-08-01 and are not live levels. The executable cost is wider than the policy gap: the CME calendar-spread cross gives a funding premium of -268.6bp annualised, 43.6bp beyond the 225bp differential, so basis and term effects pay a rolled long CAD/CHF position rather than taxing it. Transmission is direct and mechanical — this is a classic funding-versus-high-yielder cross and the franc is the funding leg. What qualifies the stance tactically is event asymmetry rather than level: the Bank of Canada decides on 2026-10-28 with a Monetary Policy Report, while the SNB has nothing scheduled until 2026-12-10, so inside four weeks only one leg can reprice, and the Canadian two-year carries roughly 112bp of hike premium above its own policy rate against a CHF two-year carrying roughly 31bp. The premium at risk is therefore some three to four times larger on the CAD side, which caps confidence at 56 despite a differential that is not going to move at all in the window.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the question is whether the 225bp gap widens or narrows, and the probability distribution is modestly in CAD's favour even though both dossiers judge their own curve too hawkish. The Bank of Canada sits at the bottom of a 2.25-3.25% neutral band and has two scheduled decisions inside the horizon, with the base-currency dossier putting one 25bp move at most at meaningful probability and a hike-plus-signal outcome at roughly 25%. The SNB sits at a zero floor with exactly one scheduled assessment on 2026-12-10, and the quote dossier puts a hike there at roughly 20% against market pricing near 50%. So the more likely single-step change is a BoC hike, which widens the gap to 250bp, rather than an SNB hike, which narrows it to 200bp. Meanwhile the carry accrues: 225bp of policy differential, or 268.6bp on the executable roll, is roughly 112-134bp of return over six months on a cross whose 3M at-the-money vol is estimated at 4.997%, giving a carry-to-vol ratio of about 0.45 on the policy basis and 0.54 on the roll. Against that, the Canadian two-year has far more premium to surrender than the Swiss, and the SNB cannot ease below zero, so the floor under CHF rates is hard while the Canadian front end has 112bp of air beneath it. Net: Bullish, but on accrual and on a mildly favourable step distribution rather than on any expectation that the gap widens materially.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The growth differential is the widest single macro gap in this pair and it runs against CAD. Switzerland grew 1.885% quarter on quarter and 2.632% year on year in Q2 2026, the fastest quarterly rate in the G10+SGD set; Canada grew 0.82% quarter on quarter and 1.13% year on year, the second weakest in the same set. The momentum gap is sharper still: Switzerland's September data tally was six positive surprises and zero negative on the vendor's own direction flag, with KOF at a five-year high of 109.1 against a 105.8 consensus, while Canada's September tally was eight negative and six positive, with employment falling 41,700 against a +15,100 forecast and permanent-employee wage growth halving to 2.0%. Canadian unemployment at 6.4% is more than double Switzerland's 3.1% registered rate. The inflation side partially offsets: Canadian headline CPI at 3.0% and operational core at 1.95% sit 220bp and 155bp above Swiss headline at 0.8% and core at 0.4%, and that core gap is what keeps the 225bp policy differential defensible. But the transmission inside four weeks runs through data surprise rather than through reaction functions, and Canada has two high-leverage prints — the 2026-10-09 labour report and the 2026-10-19 CPI — against a Swiss calendar containing only a CPI print and an unemployment reading that the SECO forecast already pins at 3.1%. The asymmetry of disappointment is Canadian.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the growth gap widens rather than closes, because the two economies face opposite policy shocks. Governor Macklem has put Canadian Q4 growth 'below 1%' if tariffs persist, and they have not merely persisted — US Section 338 measures escalated from a 50% ad valorem duty to outright import bans effective 2026-09-29, against roughly C$20bn of Canadian retaliation imposed 2026-09-08. SECO has moved the other way, raising Swiss 2026 growth to 1.7% from 0.9% and holding 2027 at 1.6%. On inflation the two converge downward but from very different starting points and for different reasons: Canadian headline decays mechanically as gasoline's +22.8% year-on-year contribution rolls off toward the 2.4% ex-gasoline rate and then the 1.95% trim-median, while Swiss headline decays from 0.8% toward the SNB's own 0.7% path and SECO's 0.6% panel forecast as the energy base effect fades. The bilateral core gap of 155bp therefore survives the horizon roughly intact, which protects the rate differential — that belongs to Factor 1. What this factor measures is the relative cyclical position, and a tariff-shocked economy with 6.4% unemployment, benchmark house prices down 3.0% year on year and building permits down 17.3% month on month is in a materially worse cyclical position than one growing at the fastest rate in the block with 3.1% unemployment. Confidence is held at 60 because SECO itself flags that roughly half of Swiss Q2 growth came from the volatile chemical-pharmaceutical sector and because the ZEW expectations index collapsed to 2.6 from 12.1.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is a moderate risk-on pair: CHF is the safe haven and CAD the commodity-linked growth proxy, so the pair rises when risk appetite holds and falls when capital flees to the franc. The current tape denies the franc its mechanism. VIX closed at 16.07 on 2026-09-28, in the lower third of its distribution and up only 1.64 points over the month; the S&P 500 is up 14.33% year to date and within 1.8% of its record; US investment-grade spreads at 83bp are historically tight. Gold corroborates: XAU/USD fell 6.00% over the month, and because the franc's only commodity link runs through shared safe-haven demand rather than trade, a gold unwind is a franc unwind measured a second way. RBC's August Currency Report Card frames the same point from the other side, describing the franc as the most efficient short leg in G10 carry precisely because volatility is subdued and noting that the brief safe-haven bid during peak Iran tensions failed to gain traction. The asymmetry that keeps confidence at 58 rather than higher is that the risk channel is not symmetric for this pair: CAD's own equity correlation is the weakest in the commodity bloc at -0.2 to -0.3 on USD/CAD versus the S&P, so a benign tape gives the pair only a modest lift, while a genuine risk event gives the franc a large and non-linear bid. Two counterweights are already visible — US high-yield spreads 42bp wider over the month to 302bp, and the OAT-Bund spread at a one-year high of 111.2bp — but neither is corroborated elsewhere in the risk complex.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the stance flattens to Neutral because the distribution becomes two-sided in a way the modal path conceals. Two named binaries sit inside the horizon and both resolve against this pair if they resolve badly: the Iran conflict, at day 215 on 2026-09-30 with the US having rejected Iran's seven-day roadmap and the residual dispute reduced to sequencing; and France, where 111.2bp over Bunds, 119% debt to GDP and a EUR 54bn budget vote make a government collapse a live possibility and the franc rather than the euro is the regional refuge. The franc's payoff to either is large and non-linear — the January 2015 floor removal moved EUR/CHF roughly 30% intraday is the quote dossier's own reference — while the pair's upside from a continued benign tape is linear and modest. Against that, the CAD leg has its own unhelpful geometry: an Iran settlement that collapses the oil premium is risk-positive but terms-of-trade negative for Canada, so the pair does not cleanly monetise good geopolitical news either. The honest resolution is a wide, roughly symmetric distribution in expectation with an asymmetric shape — most paths deliver nothing for this factor and a minority deliver a sharp fall. Confidence is 52 because the correlation regime itself is unreliable this cycle: gold fell 6.00% while VIX rose 1.64 points, which is not the standard shared-safe-haven structure.

Over four weeks the probability that a volatility regime shift occurs and completes is low, so the benign tape simply lets the carry work and the pair drifts up. Over six months two dated negotiations have time to fail, and the franc's payoff to failure is large enough and non-linear enough that an expectation-weighted stance is Neutral even though the modal path is unchanged. Pass-2 note (does not alter the scored stance): This factor's tactical Bullish rests on a calm tape with OAT-Bund at 111.2bp. Since then the OAT/Bund spread reached 130.3bp on Oct 1, up 13.2bp from the previous session, and reports put it at 141bp, the widest since 2012. That is the French-stress channel this factor's strategic Neutral was built around, and it fired inside the tactical window. We record this as the single largest reason we disagree with the tactical Neutral.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Speculators are net short BOTH legs, which is the configuration that mutes rather than amplifies a pair signal. Canadian dollar leveraged funds were net short 46,861 contracts in the 2026-09-22 tranche, 15.1% of 311,085 open interest; Swiss franc leveraged funds were net short 16,457 contracts in the same tranche, 12.3% of 133,495. A short on both sides nets to very little directional information for the cross. The composition differs in ways that pull in opposite directions and roughly cancel. On the CAD side the short has been halved from 88,897 over five weeks and was covered INTO Canadian dollar weakness, so the squeeze fuel is largely spent and the room to rebuild toward -89k exceeds the room to cover to flat. On the CHF side the short was built for five consecutive weeks into 2026-09-22 — but the subsequent week, to 2026-09-29, saw specs cover 2,462 contracts to a net -13,995 with open interest essentially flat at 133,872, and on a ten-year basis that position sits at the 36.1 flip percentile with a z-score of -0.48, which the source itself describes as not crowded. That materially weakens the franc-squeeze asymmetry the quote dossier identified from the 2026-09-22 snapshot alone. With neither leg at a genuine ten-year extreme and both covering, the pair-level signal is noise.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months positioning carries no directional content for this cross and the weight falls to 0.06 for that reason. Both legs are structurally short by construction rather than by conviction: the franc has been net short in every tranche of the cached 2026-04 to 2026-09 sample because it is a funding currency, and the Canadian dollar short sits inside its own brief's significance band of +40k to -80k with no extreme to revert from. Any squeeze on either leg is followed by a rebuild, because the carry that justified the short — 225bp of it between these two currencies — does not change. Pair-specific flow structure is thin: CAD/CHF has no listed option anywhere, so there is no option-hedging flow, no barrier interest and no dealer gamma to speak of, and the cross is traded through the two dollar legs rather than directly. There are no identifiable bilateral capital flows of scale: Swiss reserve managers hold no meaningful CAD allocation and CHF accounts for 0.19% of allocated global reserves, flat over five years. The one agent capable of taking the other side at scale is the SNB, and its reaction function is asymmetric — it intervenes to cap franc strength, not weakness, and dropped the 'increased' intervention qualifier in September. That removes an official bid from under the franc but equally means no official seller appears unless the franc rallies hard.

factors.horizon_split: Neutral on both horizons with confidence easing from 55 to 52. The tactical Neutral is a genuine cancellation — two short legs of similar relative size, both covering, neither at a ten-year extreme. The strategic Neutral is a statement that the question itself has no answer at six months, because both positions are structural resting states rather than deviations, and the lower confidence prices the absence of any pair-level positioning series at all.

tactical.combined_positioning_signal: Net short both legs — CAD -15.1% and CHF -12.3% of their respective open interest — which mutes the cross signal. Netted, there is no crowded CAD/CHF trade in either direction.
tactical.unwind_trigger: A VIX close above 24, an OAT-Bund break through 125bp on a French no-confidence vote, or a public failure of the Iran negotiation. Each forces franc covering, and because CAD shorts are already half-covered the pair would fall further than a symmetric read of the two books implies. Pass-2 note: the tactical unwind trigger named above, an OAT-Bund break through 125bp, was met on 2026-10-01. The pair's 120-pip fall over two sessions fits the described mechanism. No post-2026-09-29 CFTC print was available to confirm franc covering.
tactical.historical_analogue: The August-to-September Canadian dollar episode is the instructive one: 42,036 contracts of CAD shorts were bought back and produced no CAD appreciation at all. Covering without appreciation is a bearish tell for the covered currency, and the franc has just begun the same pattern, covering 2,462 contracts in the week to 2026-09-29 without a franc rally.
tactical.contrarian_case: The crowd is short both currencies and is quietly getting out of both, which means the marginal flow is two-way and the pair has lost whatever squeeze asymmetry it had a month ago. The contrarian trade here is not to fade either leg but to refuse to pay for a squeeze in a cross where the franc sits at the 36th percentile of ten years and the Canadian dollar 27,000 contracts inside its own extreme threshold.

strategic.historical_analogue: The franc's post-2024 funding-currency regime, in which short positions rebuilt after every risk-off squeeze because the rate differential that justified them never changed. The quote dossier's own sample shows no long observation in any tranche.
strategic.contrarian_case: The genuine contrarian risk is not a speculative squeeze but an official one. The SNB is the only agent that could take the other side of a combined short book at scale, and its reaction function is asymmetric — it caps franc strength and tolerates weakness, which is why it dropped the 'increased' intervention language in September. That asymmetry means a weakening franc gets no official bid, but it also means a sharply strengthening franc meets intervention rather than a rate cut, which is a less credible deterrent and sustains the optionality the market keeps paying for.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Strategic adjusted from 0.16 default; +0.01 strategic only. The bilateral current-account gap of 8.17pp of GDP (CHF +9.198% vs CAD +1.03%) is among the widest between any two G10 currencies, and the two external positions have opposite structures — one a structurally entrenched surplus on pharma, financial services and primary income, the other a price-driven surplus on energy exports that is already reversing.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both dossiers score their own external balance Neutral tactically, and for this cross the reasons genuinely cancel. Switzerland's Q2 current account surplus of 9.198% of GDP is eight times Canada's 1.03%, but the high-frequency Swiss trade balance narrowed to CHF 3.786bn in the 2026-09-17 release from CHF 5.742bn, and Canada's July merchandise balance collapsed to +C$0.77bn from +C$4.2bn against a +C$3.2bn forecast — both monthly series are deteriorating at once. The direct bilateral channel is immaterial: IMF DOTS puts Canadian goods exports to Switzerland at USD 4.6bn and imports from Switzerland at USD 5.8bn in 2024, for a Canadian net goods deficit of USD 1.2bn, against total Canadian goods exports of which 66.3% went to the United States in July 2026. Note that the mirror data disagree — Switzerland reports importing USD 8.5bn from Canada against Canada's reported USD 4.6bn of exports — which is the standard precious-metals asymmetry in Swiss trade statistics, since precious metals were 39.9% of Swiss goods exports in 2025. Either way the flow is too small to move a cross at a four-week horizon. Commodity netting is the live channel and it is mildly pair-positive: Brent at approximately USD 100.17 on 2026-10-01 is +4.75% over September, which is mildly CAD-supportive and mildly CHF-negative for a net energy importer, while gold down 6.00% over the month removes a franc support.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.17 strategic weight this is the second-heaviest factor and the differential is one-sided. Switzerland's surplus is structurally entrenched across three independent legs — a goods surplus from pharmaceuticals and precision manufacturing, a services surplus from financial services and commodity trading, and primary income on a CHF 5,564bn stock of foreign assets supporting a net international investment position of CHF 986bn — and it widened by CHF 13bn year on year in Q2 to CHF 24bn. RBC's August Currency Report Card names the same surplus as the structural bull case for the franc. Canada's surplus is a single-leg, price-driven artefact: the entire swing from -C$8.3bn to +C$8.8bn came from goods, on record energy exports of C$60.6bn, and the Reuters September poll puts 2026 WTI at USD 83.90, below the USD 91.51 print of 2026-09-30. Worse, Canada cannot monetise the global crude premium — Brent traded USD 11.05 above WTI on 2026-09-30 against USD 4.08 a year earlier, and WCS settles USD 14.80 under WTI, so the realised Canadian barrel is near USD 76.70 against a USD 100.17 headline. Layer on Section 338 import bans taxing exactly the goods balance that produced the surplus, and the Canadian external position shrinks over the horizon while the Swiss one persists. Commodity netting partially offsets and is the reason this is 62 rather than 70: oil higher is modestly CAD-positive and modestly CHF-negative, so a sustained energy shock works for the pair even as the balance-of-payments arithmetic works against it.

factors.horizon_split: Neutral tactically and Bearish strategically, with the weight rising from 0.06 to 0.17 — so the stance change and the weight change compound. Balance-of-payments flows accumulate rather than arrive, and over four weeks both monthly series are deteriorating together, which cancels. Over six months the composition dominates the direction: a three-legged structural Swiss surplus does not reverse, while a single-legged Canadian surplus built on a reversing oil price and taxed by live import bans does.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: CAD: crude oil (WTI/WCS-linked, not Brent), natural gas, forestry and base metals. Energy exports were a record C$60.6bn in Q2 2026 with crude and bitumen at C$44.8bn, so the Canadian dollar's commodity exposure is large, direct and concentrated in oil — but realised at WTI less a USD 14.80 WCS discount, not at the Brent headline.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: CHF: no direct commodity export exposure at all. Switzerland is a net energy importer with energy at roughly 3.5% of its CPI basket, and precious metals are 39.9% of its 2025 goods exports but overwhelmingly as refining and transit rather than domestic production. The only genuine commodity link is COMEX gold, and it runs through shared safe-haven demand rather than through trade.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Applying the framework's direction rules: Oil up gives +CAD (mild, per the rules, and milder still here because the Brent-WTI spread of USD 11.05 and the USD 14.80 WCS discount mean Canada captures only part of any waterborne move) and -CHF (mild, as a net energy importer, but damped by energy's 3.5% basket weight against roughly 7% in the eurozone). Net of the two mild effects, oil up is BULLISH CAD/CHF, but weakly — perhaps a quarter of the sensitivity a clean petro-versus-importer pair would show. Gold up gives +CHF through the safe-haven correlation and is neutral for CAD, so gold up is BEARISH CAD/CHF. Natural gas and LNG are immaterial to both legs bilaterally. The dominant netting conclusion is that CAD/CHF is a much weaker commodity pair than its constituents suggest: the base currency cannot monetise the headline oil price and the quote currency barely feels it.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Brent from approximately USD 100 to USD 110 with the Brent-WTI spread intact: CAD gains mildly on terms of trade but the realised Canadian barrel rises only to about USD 84, and a supply-driven rally would also lift the franc through the risk channel if it came with an Iran escalation. Net pair impact: mildly bullish CAD/CHF, materially less than the 10% commodity move implies, and ambiguous if the move is supply- rather than demand-driven.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Brent to approximately USD 90 on an Iran settlement: CAD loses on terms of trade and the Canadian current-account surplus shrinks faster toward the C$2-5bn path, while the franc loses its safe-haven bid and its energy-driven inflation impulse simultaneously. Both legs weaken, so the net pair impact is close to flat — which is the clearest single statement of why this factor's commodity leg does not rescue the Canadian dollar.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: The Brent-WTI spread and the WCS differential, not the oil price itself. They determine whether a given crude level reaches Canadian export revenue at all, and at USD 11.05 and USD 14.80 respectively they are currently blocking most of it. Gold is the secondary driver, acting only on the CHF leg.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks face the same structural problem — a market pricing more tightening than the bank's own published view supports — but the magnitudes and the timetables differ, and both differences run against this pair. Governor Macklem pivoted openly hawkish in Halifax on 2026-09-21, warning against being 'too slow to respond', but tied the inflation call explicitly to oil staying near USD 100 per barrel; WTI closed at USD 91.51 on 2026-09-30, 8.5% below that threshold, and the Reuters 2026 WTI consensus is USD 83.90. The precondition has failed, and the Bank must publish a forecast against it at the 2026-10-28 Monetary Policy Report, which also debuts a new inflation model. The SNB's equivalent gap is wider in probability terms — the market prices nearly a 50% chance of a December hike against a conditional forecast of 0.7%/0.8%/0.8% built explicitly on an unchanged 0% rate — but it cannot resolve inside the tactical window, because the SNB does not meet until 2026-12-10. So the only guidance event available in four weeks is a Canadian one with dovish risk attached, set against 112bp of embedded hike premium in the Canadian two-year versus roughly 31bp in the Swiss. Sequencing compounds it: the Bank of Canada speaks twice (2026-10-28 and 2026-12-09) before the SNB speaks once, and the second Canadian decision falls the day before the Swiss one, so Canada sets the tone into the Swiss assessment rather than the reverse.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices the Halifax language as a commitment and carries roughly two Bank of Canada hikes by January 2027, while pricing a coin flip on the SNB that cannot be tested until December. The Canadian half of that is testable on 2026-10-28 and the Swiss half is not.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months both wedges resolve and both resolutions, on the dossiers' own probabilities, point the same way for this cross. The Bank of Canada must reconcile a 3.0% headline with a 1.95% trim-median core, 6.4% unemployment, wage growth halved to 2.0% and an economy Governing Council describes as still in excess supply; the base dossier expects one 25bp move at most against roughly 50bp priced over the window, and Scotiabank — the most CAD-constructive major house — already publishes 75bp against the curve's 120bp. The SNB must reconcile a 0.8% headline and a 0.4% core with market pricing of at least 0.75% by September 2027; the quote dossier expects a hold and notes 60% of a Swiss Bankers Association survey sees no change through 2027. Both banks are expected to disappoint, but the Canadian disappointment is roughly three to four times larger in embedded basis points and lands first. Credibility differs too: the SNB has the best inflation record in the developed world and publishes a three-year conditional forecast, while the Bank of Canada has just conditioned its bias on an oil price that has already failed, which is the more fragile communication. Confidence is 58 rather than higher because the 2026-12-10 assessment is a genuine coin flip on the market's own numbers, and an SNB hike there would be the single cleanest way this factor's conclusion inverts.

We expect both to disappoint and the Canadian disappointment to be the larger and the earlier, which is a net negative for the pair even though both disappointments are individually currency-negative.

factors.horizon_split: Bearish on both horizons at the same 58 confidence, which is unusual and deliberate. The factor's tactical and strategic content are the same disagreement observed at different resolutions: tactically the asymmetry is pure timing, because only the Bank of Canada speaks; strategically it is pure magnitude, because the Canadian front end has three to four times the premium to surrender. The confidence does not decay because the 2026-12-10 SNB coin flip, which is the main source of error, is a strategic risk that the tactical window does not even contain.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Event risk on this cross is asymmetric in an unusual way: the Canadian leg carries realised, already-enacted damage while the Swiss leg carries unrealised optionality, and both point the pair the same direction. On the base side, US Section 338 measures escalated from a 50% ad valorem duty to outright import bans effective 2026-09-29 at 12:01 ET, covering dairy, alcoholic beverages and motor vehicles, with USMCA providing no relief and the duties stacking on existing AD/CVD and Section 232 measures; Canada retaliated on 2026-09-08 with roughly C$20bn of tariffs. That is a live shock to an economy sending 66.3% of its goods exports to one counterparty, and it will show in the 2026-10-06 trade print and the 2026-10-09 labour report. On the quote side, Switzerland's domestic political risk is effectively nil — stable federal government, no election inside the horizon, the EU Bilaterals III package not entering force before end-2028 — while the franc holds free options on two live external binaries, the Iran negotiation at day 215 and a French budget vote with OAT-Bund at a one-year high of 111.2bp. A currency with no domestic event risk and two free call options against a currency absorbing an enacted trade shock is a bearish configuration for CAD/CHF.

tactical.what_is_priced: The tariff regime is priced as a known level rather than an evolving process — Canada's REER fell 1.67 points over twelve months while AUD's rose 9.97 — and the two Swiss-relevant binaries are priced as resolving benignly. Neither the 2026-10-06 trade print nor the 2026-10-09 labour report carries a tariff-damage expectation.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the Canadian trade architecture is the structural negative and it has got worse, not better: the United States declined the 16-year USMCA extension at the 2026-07-01 joint review, so the agreement now runs on annual review cycles through to a 2036 expiry, converting a settled treaty into a permanently renegotiated one for the most trade-concentrated economy in the G10. US demands include 50% of North American vehicle value originating in the United States, and 62% of Canadians support retaliation, so there is no easy concession path. Switzerland has no comparable exposure. But the strategic stance is materially less confident than the tactical one, at 54, because both of the horizon's largest binaries can resolve in the pair's favour. An Iran settlement — the modal path, with regional crude exports back to just under 80% of pre-war and the dispute reduced to sequencing — would be doubly franc-negative, removing the safe-haven bid and the energy-driven inflation impulse behind SNB hike pricing at once, and only mildly CAD-negative through a terms-of-trade channel Canada barely captures anyway. A USTR-Canada interim deal by the stated end-2026 target would lift the Canadian leg directly. Those two outcomes together carry meaningful probability and both are bullish for the cross, which is why a factor with a one-sided structural story carries only 54 confidence.

What is not priced on the Canadian side is permanence — an annually renegotiated USMCA is a standing risk premium rather than a one-off shock.

factors.horizon_split: Bearish on both horizons with confidence falling from 60 to 54. Tactically the Canadian shock is enacted and dated — import bans two days before the valuation date, with damage due in two prints inside four weeks — while the Swiss options are free and unexpired. Strategically the same Canadian structure persists, but the two largest binaries in the horizon both have benign resolutions that would be bullish for the cross, and an Iran settlement in particular hits the franc twice while barely touching the Canadian dollar, so the expectation-weighted case softens considerably.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Neither sovereign generates an FX signal inside four weeks and the high confidence reflects how clearly the evidence supports that. Switzerland is rated AAA or Aaa by all five agencies with stable outlooks and runs a federal budget balance of 0.00% of GDP under a constitutional debt brake; Canada carries Aaa from Moody's, AAA from S&P and DBRS and AA+ from Fitch, all stable, with no agency on review. There is a rating differential — Fitch's 2024 downgrade left Canada one notch below Switzerland at one of four agencies — but a single-notch gap between two AAA-equivalent sovereigns does not move a currency pair. Neither curve shows stress: Swiss benchmarks at 0.31% (2y) and 0.58% (10y) and Canadian benchmarks at 3.37% and 3.96% both slope smoothly upward, with the Canadian 2s10s at +59bp and the Swiss at +27bp, and neither contains an identifiable credit premium. No budget, fiscal update or scheduled rating review falls inside the tactical window for either sovereign. The only live tactical datum is Canada's monthly budget balance of -C$4.77bn reported 2026-09-25 against +C$0.99bn prior, which is a real deterioration and an order of magnitude too small to matter on a cross.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.07 strategic weight this becomes the one place where the two sovereigns' trajectories genuinely diverge, and the divergence is one of the widest in the G10. Swiss general government gross debt is falling — 40.5% of GDP in 2024, 39.4% in 2025, 38.5% projected for 2026 and 33.5% by 2031 — under a constitutional debt brake that makes the path a rule rather than a forecast. Canadian general government debt is rising on the same measure, from 88.6% in 2024 to 91.8% in 2026 and a projected 98.5% in 2027 against an AA median of 49.6%, with the general government deficit at 3.3% of GDP against an AA median of 2.3% and a pre-2019 two-decade Canadian average of 0.4%. Fitch's assessment, though 322 days old and flagged stale by the base dossier, warns that persistent fiscal expansion has weakened the credit profile. The base dossier puts the probability of a Fitch or Moody's negative action inside six months at 15%; the equivalent Swiss probability is effectively zero. Confidence is held at 50 — the lowest in this analysis — because neither market is repricing any of this, Canadian federal debt at 42.4% of GDP remains low in absolute terms, and the Canadian fiscal space is being spent on tariff-support programmes the Bank of Canada expects to mitigate real harm. This is a direction-of-travel stance at a small weight, not a claim that sovereign risk is about to matter.

The dominant negative mechanism is that the Canadian dollar is the weaker leg on everything that is not a policy rate: Q2 growth of 0.82% quarter on quarter against Switzerland's 1.885%, unemployment of 6.4% against 3.1%, eight negative September data surprises against Switzerland's zero, and a Section 338 import-ban regime that took effect two days before the valuation date with no Swiss analogue. Path of least resistance over four weeks is therefore carry accrual interrupted by Canadian data, with the dated catalysts being the 2026-10-06 trade print, the 2026-10-09 labour report, the 2026-10-19 CPI and the 2026-10-28 decision. Conviction is 2 because a Neutral score built from a real cancellation is a statement that the pair has no tactical direction, not that the analysis is thin.

consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Neutral. Net weighted score +0.0706, conviction 2, overall confidence 54. Carry and a benign risk regime offset Canadian data and event asymmetry almost exactly over four weeks.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bearish. Net weighted score -0.1350, conviction 2, overall confidence 56. The external-balance gap, the guidance asymmetry and the growth differential outweigh a 225bp carry that is the Canadian dollar's only strategic support.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: No major-bank CAD/CHF pair forecast was located (thin and partly unavailable, reported as such). The only aggregate found, Exchange Rates UK's two-provider CHF/CAD path, is effectively one house and not a bank consensus; it inverts to CAD/CHF near 0.5798, 0.5746, 0.5746 and 0.5793 for Q4 2026 to Q3 2027. Strategically we are broadly in line with that thin aggregate, which also has CAD/CHF modestly below the payload spot into Q1 2027; tactically we are less directional than it, as it carries a continuous downward drift where we see a cancellation. On the carry framing we are in line with RBC (Currency Report Card, 13 August 2026) that carry remains the dominant theme in low vol and CHF the most efficient short leg, but we weight the base currency's structural deterioration more heavily than a pure carry framework would.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Small and poorly measurable. The two-provider aggregate implies roughly -0.6% to -0.7% from the payload spot by Q1 2027; our strategic score of -0.1350 is a direction without a magnitude in this pass, since levels belong to pass 2. The more meaningful divergence is against the rates market, where we are roughly 25-50bp below Canadian pricing over six months and roughly 50-75bp below Swiss pricing, with the Canadian gap the larger in basis points and the earlier in time.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: The pure carry framing that RBC and the broader market apply treats the franc as the short leg and stops there, which produces a mechanical long bias in any cross where the franc is the quote currency. We weight two bilateral factors more heavily than that framing does. First, the external-balance composition: a 9.198%-of-GDP Swiss surplus built on three structurally entrenched legs and a 1.03% Canadian surplus built on one price-driven leg are not the same object scaled, and at a 0.17 strategic weight the difference in durability matters more than the difference in level. Second, the asymmetry of embedded front-end premium: the Canadian two-year carries roughly 112bp above its policy rate against the Swiss two-year's 31bp, so when both central banks disappoint — which both dossiers expect — the pair falls, and the Bank of Canada gets to disappoint first and twice. The carry framing also underweights that Canada is absorbing an enacted trade shock, with Section 338 import bans live since 2026-09-29 inside an annually renegotiated USMCA, while Switzerland faces no equivalent. Pass-2 research addendum: SNB pricing is less settled than the verdict assumes; with September CPI at 1.0%, the July-September average matches the SNB's 0.7% Q3 forecast and the path then requires Q4 inflation to average 1.2%, one analyst judges a December hold remains the base case but risks are skewed towards tightening, and Lombard Odier reads the September assessment as opening the door to a possible December rise (OCBC takes the opposite side, the CHF dossier's own view). These sources, the 1.0% Swiss print and the OAT-Bund move through 140bp all arrived after pass 1 struck the tactical Neutral; we think they push the tactical risk toward the downside, weakening the 'benign tape' premise of Factor 3's tactical Bullish and the dollar-funding premise of Factor 10, so we call it a Neutral with a bearish skew. The scored verdict stands as issued, and our disagreement is carried only in scenario expected value (-6 pips before carry) and in the conviction-ladder thresholds. The bank house view on the franc leg is also turning: Rabobank raised its nine- to 12-month EUR/CHF forecast to 0.95 from 0.94 in August, a franc-weakness call that the French stress is now testing, with EUR/CHF at a two-month low near 0.9300 as investors rushed into the franc. Retail model forecasts (Traders Union, 30rates, LongForecast, WalletInvestor, pandaforecast) were treated as category errors and not used as consensus.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: The strategic payoff accrues through a Canadian front end surrendering 112bp of hike premium against a Swiss front end surrendering 31bp, plus a Canadian current account shrinking toward C$2-5bn while the Swiss one persists. The cleaner relative-value payoff is not in this cross at all — the base dossier's CAD/NOK short and the quote dossier's EUR/CHF short each isolate one leg of the thesis with better carry characteristics than CAD/CHF offers either way.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: Two specific ways this loses. An SNB hike on 2026-12-10 — priced near 50% by the market against our roughly 20% — would reclassify the franc from funding currency to one with a cycle, compress the differential to 200bp and reverse the sign of the pair's only large positive contribution. Or WTI reclaiming USD 100 with the Brent-WTI spread narrowing inside USD 6 would simultaneously restore Macklem's stated hiking precondition and Canada's revenue capture, flipping Factors 5 and 6 together and taking the strategic score positive. Being wrong on the strategic view while short the pair also means paying away 225-269bp of carry for the privilege.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons diverge by 0.2056 of score and by one stance category, and the divergence is structural rather than noise. Four factors change between the horizons and three of them move against the pair. Inflation & Growth holds Bearish but its weight halves from 0.18 to 0.10, which actually helps the pair. External Balance moves from Neutral to Bearish while its weight rises from 0.06 to 0.17, a swing of -0.1054 that is single-handedly larger than the entire tactical score. Guidance holds Bearish while its weight rises from 0.07 to 0.12. Fiscal moves from Neutral to Bearish at a rising weight. Working the other way, Risk Appetite gives up a +0.0638 tactical positive as the two binaries gain time to resolve, and USD Liquidity gives up +0.0378. So the carry contribution is roughly constant across horizons while the structural negatives accumulate — which is exactly what should happen to a positive-carry cross whose base currency is deteriorating: carry is a rate of accrual and deterioration is a stock that builds.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 2026-12-09 and 2026-12-10 pair of decisions, with the Bank of Canada deciding one session before the SNB's quarterly assessment. That 48-hour window is where the tactical cancellation resolves into the strategic direction: the Bank of Canada either validates or surrenders the 112bp of premium in its two-year, and the SNB then either validates or removes the roughly 75bp the market has priced into its own path. The earlier 2026-10-28 Monetary Policy Report is the first test but cannot resolve the Swiss half, because the SNB has no scheduled communication before December.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: The two horizons should not be run as one position. The tactical Neutral is not a trade — a +0.0706 score on a cross with no listed option and 225bp of carry says the honest tactical action is to collect the carry or do nothing, not to take direction. The strategic Bearish is a trade but an awkward one in this cross specifically, because expressing it in spot means paying away 225-269bp annualised while waiting, and no option exists on CAD/CHF to convert that into a defined-premium structure. The practical consequence is that the strategic view is better expressed through the legs the dossiers each name as cleanest — short CAD against a high-yielding commodity peer, or short CHF against a higher-yielding European peer — rather than by shorting a cross where the carry runs against the thesis. Pass-2 execution note: if the strategic view is taken in the cross itself, the levels give the only entry with positive carry-adjusted expected value: sell 0.5865-0.5875, stop on a daily close above 0.5930, targets 0.5760 and 0.5700. Of the two leg alternatives named in pass 1, only the short-CAD leg expresses this pair's bearish direction; the short-CHF-against-a-European-peer alternative would be a bet against the franc, the opposite of this pair's bearish leg, so a long CHF/JPY (the quote dossier's cleanest bullish-franc expression) is the consistent franc-leg alternative.

catalysts.rationale: August printed 3.1% seasonally adjusted and 3.0% unadjusted against a SECO annual forecast of 3.1%, so a matching print carries no policy impulse. catalysts.event: SNB foreign currency reserves for September 2026
catalysts.rationale: The monthly intervention check, against August reserves of CHF 770.1bn and official reserve assets of CHF 901.6bn. A large build would imply franc selling and cap the quote leg, supporting CAD/CHF; a decline would imply reserve sales and an official franc bid against it. With gold down 6.00% over the month a flat or lower print is more likely valuation than policy, so the read is genuinely two-sided for the cross.

catalysts.event: Canada Labour Force Survey for September, released the same day as US non-farm payrolls
catalysts.rationale: August employment fell 41,700 against a +15,100 forecast with permanent-employee wage growth halving to 2.0%. A second negative print pushes unemployment above 6.6% and forces hike premium out of the Canadian two-year, which is directly bearish for CAD/CHF because no Swiss event can offset it inside the window. A sharp rebound restores the Canadian tightening case and is the single cleanest tactical positive available for the pair.

catalysts.event: French National Assembly debate and vote on the 2027 budget package (pass-2 addition; dated to the second week of October because no fixed vote date was located, date field approximate)
catalysts.rationale: Skewed Bearish. Even if the EUR 43 billion package passes intact, the deficit only falls from 5.4% to 5.0% of GDP while debt climbs to 121.7%, so passing it brings relief, not resolution. A failed or diluted vote extends the franc safe-haven bid that has already taken CAD/CHF 120 pips lower in two sessions. Passing it would ease the bid and is the likeliest trigger for the tactical upside case.

Headline held at 3.0% in August on gasoline at +22.8% year on year with the trim-median operational core at 1.95%, below target. As the fuel base effect rolls off, headline should decay toward the 2.4% ex-gasoline rate, which undercuts the roughly 120bp of Bank of Canada tightening in the curve. For the cross this is the Factor 2 and Factor 6 channels firing together, and the Swiss core at 0.40% means the bilateral core gap narrows from the Canadian side.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision with Monetary Policy Report, debuting a new inflation model (gated calendar; Monetary Policy Report flagged)
catalysts.rationale: The highest-leverage dated event in the tactical window and the only scheduled policy communication from either central bank before December. The Bank must publish an oil assumption against Macklem's 2026-09-21 statement that inflation would edge up if oil stayed near USD 100, while WTI closed at USD 91.51. Lowering that assumption is a dovish revision against a Canadian two-year carrying roughly 112bp of premium, and because the SNB does not meet until 2026-12-10 the repricing is entirely one-sided for the cross.

The cross trades through USD/CAD and USD/CHF, and the softer US data have changed the odds: cooling PCE lowered the implied probability of an October hike from nearly 51% to about 38%. A Fed skip weakens the dollar more against the franc, the haven-and-funding leg whose shorts unwind, than against CAD, whose US export exposure caps its upside. Net effect: mildly bearish for CAD/CHF.

catalysts.event: Swiss October CPI (FSO) (pass-2 addition; dated to the first week of November, exact date approximate)
catalysts.rationale: Bearish if headline reaches 1.2% or above. The SNB's own path needs Q4 inflation to average about 1.2%. An October print at or above that level, with core at or above 0.6%, validates December hike pricing and strengthens the franc against a Canadian front end already giving back premium. A print below 0.9% would partly remove Swiss hike pricing and support the pair.

catalysts.event: Canada Q3 2026 GDP and monthly GDP for September (Statistics Canada; date follows the end-of-month cadence and is not in the gated calendar)
catalysts.rationale: Q2 grew 3.3% annualised but monthly tracking stalled at 0.0% then +0.2%, and Q3 is the first full quarter under the Section 338 duty regime begun 2026-08-22. A print below 1.5% annualised would confirm the fragility Governing Council flagged and widen the growth differential against Switzerland's SECO-upgraded 1.7% path, which is the Factor 2 strategic channel.

catalysts.event: Swiss Q3 2026 GDP (SECO; date follows the cadence that produced the Q2 release on 2026-09-03 and is not in the gated calendar)
catalysts.rationale: Q2 grew 1.885% quarter on quarter, the fastest in the block, but SECO flags that roughly half came from the volatile chemical-pharmaceutical sector and expects second-half moderation. A reversion toward the 1.6% annual trend would narrow the growth gap that is this pair's main structural negative, so a soft Swiss Q3 is one of the few scheduled events that works for CAD/CHF.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision (gated calendar; no Monetary Policy Report)
catalysts.rationale: The second of two Canadian decisions inside the horizon and the one that falls the session before the SNB's assessment, so Canada sets the tone into the Swiss meeting. If the Bank has still not moved by this date the market's roughly two-hikes-by-January pricing becomes untenable and the 112bp of premium in the Canadian two-year is most likely to be surrendered here, which is directly bearish for the cross through the rate-expectations channel.

catalysts.event: Swiss National Bank quarterly monetary policy assessment with conditional inflation forecast (gated calendar; quarterly assessment flagged)
catalysts.rationale: The only scheduled Swiss policy communication in either horizon and the single largest source of error in this analysis. The market prices nearly a 50% chance of a 25bp hike against an SNB conditional forecast of 0.7%/0.8%/0.8% built on an unchanged 0% rate. A hold with no tightening signal removes Swiss front-end premium and is bullish CAD/CHF; a hike compresses the differential to 200bp, reclassifies the franc from funding currency to one with a cycle, and reverses the sign of this pair's largest positive factor contribution.

catalysts.event: USTR target date for USMCA interim agreements
catalysts.rationale: The United States declined the 16-year USMCA extension at the 2026-07-01 joint review, placing the agreement on annual review cycles through 2036, and USTR has stated it aims to have interim deals ready by end-2026. An interim deal suspending the Section 338 import bans is the largest single CAD-positive catalyst in the horizon and the principal risk to the strategic Bearish stance; failure entrenches a standing risk premium on Canadian assets against a Swiss sovereign carrying none.

Post-verdict information: web research accessed 2026-10-06 surfaced events dated 2026-10-01 to 2026-10-05 (the OAT-Bund spread breaching 130-140bp; Swiss September CPI at 1.0% and core at 0.5%; softer US data cutting Fed October hike odds). These are used for narrative, scenario conditions and the published disagreement only and do not change any scored element. US payrolls timing is ambiguous across sources (the CAD dossier dates the next payrolls to 2026-10-09; one 2026-10-05 summary refers to a weak payrolls report already released), so no claim is made about the release date.

Implied volatility: pair_3m_iv is 4.997% at a 99.7-day tenor. It is a triangle ESTIMATE using a realised correlation of 0.6937, which the store documents as running low by a median 14.4%. No option is listed on CAD/CHF, so there is no risk reversal, IV percentile, barrier or vol-surface skew; these are structural absences and the iv_percentile field is therefore null. The CAD CFTC percentile is not published in the report and is recorded as null.

Carry sign convention: annualised_carry_bps is entered as +268.6 (the executable roll, which the report states as -268.6bp funding premium because the forward trades at a discount; a rolled long earns it). Policy differential is +225bp. carry_to_vol_ratio of 0.54 is 268.6/100/4.997; the report's 0.45 is on the 225bp policy basis.
Forward outrights are derived by linear extrapolation of the -268.6bp CME calendar-spread roll. They embed an unseparated cross-currency basis and are not quoted forward points.

Rates block: the 10-year yields (CAD 3.675%, CHF 0.47%) are monthly observations as of 2026-08-01 and are not quoted as live levels. The two-year spread signpost uses dossier live prints (Canada 3.37% on 2026-09-28, Switzerland 0.31% on 2026-09-29).

REER-relative valuation is a proxy from BIS broad real indices for 2026-08, not true purchasing-power parity. The 4.8% gap at the current spot is an approximation because the REERs predate the spot move.
Scenario probabilities follow the framework's 50/25/25 structure. Scenario levels and the derived expected values are pass-2 judgements consistent with, but not inputs to, the settled score.
Bilateral trade is the supplied IMF DOTS block, used as given. The mirror-data asymmetry is disclosed in Factor 5.
Retail model forecast sites returned by search were rejected as category errors and are not cited as consensus. Bank consensus is therefore null: no major-bank CAD/CHF pair forecast was located.

Pass-1 assumptions on CFTC vintages, the funding premium, catalyst dating, cross-currency basis gaps and oil-price reconciliation are retained unchanged. Catalyst dates for items dated only to a week (French budget vote, Swiss October CPI) are approximate.
The Exchange Rates UK CHF/CAD path (two providers, 0.0% range width) is treated as best-available aggregate, effectively one house, and not as a bank consensus.
